Test your knowledge of the material on [loglinear models](../lectures/04-Loglin.pdf) in the following quiz to see how much you learned.
This is **entirely private for you**---no records are kept of your performance. When you've answered all the questions, click on the Submit Quiz button
to see how you've done, and perhaps get pointers to things you should review.

<div class="quiz-container">

<form id="quizForm">

<div class="question" id="q1">
<h3>1. What is a loglinear model for frequency tables in categorical data analysis?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="a" id="q1a"> <label for="q1a">a) A linear regression model for categorical data</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="b" id="q1b"> <label for="q1b">b) A logistic regression model for categorical data</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="c" id="q1c"> <label for="q1c">c) A statistical model for analyzing the relationship between categorical variables</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="d" id="q1d"> <label for="q1d">d) A model for predicting binary outcomes from categorical predictors</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp1"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q2">
<h3>2. How do you test for goodness of fit of a loglinear model for a two-way frequency table?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="a" id="q2a"> <label for="q2a">a) By using a chi-squared test</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="b" id="q2b"> <label for="q2b">b) By using a likelihood ratio test</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="c" id="q2c"> <label for="q2c">c) By using a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="d" id="q2d"> <label for="q2d">d) By using Cohen's kappa</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp2"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q3">
<h3>3. What is the main difference between a <code>glm()</code> loglinear model and the chi-squared test for independence in two-way frequency tables?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q3" value="a" id="q3a"> <label for="q3a">a) <code>glm()</code> models allow for different types of associations among variables while chi-squared test only tests for independence</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q3" value="b" id="q3b"> <label for="q3b">b) <code>glm()</code> models allow for non-normal data while chi-squared tests do not</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q3" value="c" id="q3c"> <label for="q3c">c) <code>glm()</code> models apply in small sample size while chi-squared tests require large sample size</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q3" value="d" id="q3d"> <label for="q3d">d) <code>glm()</code> models allow for estimation of parameters for interactions among variables and also for non-normal data while chi-squared test only tests for independence</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp3"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q4">
<h3>4. How does a loglinear model differ from a logit model?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q4" value="a" id="q4a"> <label for="q4a">a) Loglinear models are linear while logit models are non-linear</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q4" value="b" id="q4b"> <label for="q4b">b) Logit models handle only binary outcomes while loglinear models handle more than 2 outcomes</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q4" value="c" id="q4c"> <label for="q4c">c) Loglinear models are used for continuous data while logit models are used for categorical data</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q4" value="d" id="q4d"> <label for="q4d">d) Logit models estimate probabilities while loglinear models estimate frequencies</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp4"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q5">
<h3>5. What is the difference between a loglinear model fit by <code>loglm()</code> and one fit using <code>glm()</code>?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q5" value="a" id="q5a"> <label for="q5a">a) <code>loglm()</code> requires large samples while <code>glm()</code> can be used for smaller samples</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q5" value="b" id="q5b"> <label for="q5b">b) <code>loglm()</code> only estimates fitted values while <code>glm()</code> estimates parameters</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q5" value="c" id="q5c"> <label for="q5c">c) <code>loglm()</code> uses an iterative process while <code>glm()</code> provides an exact solution</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q5" value="d" id="q5d"> <label for="q5d">d) <code>loglm()</code> gives the Pearson chi-square test while <code>glm()</code> gives the likelihood ratio test</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp5"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q6">
<h3>6. What are the advantages of a loglinear model fit using <code>glm()</code> over one fit using <code>loglm()</code>?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q6" value="a" id="q6a"> <label for="q6a">a) <code>glm()</code> estimates parameters while <code>loglm()</code> estimates only fitted values</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q6" value="b" id="q6b"> <label for="q6b">b) <code>glm()</code> can handle ordinal and quantitative predictors while <code>loglm()</code> cannot</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q6" value="c" id="q6c"> <label for="q6c">c) <code>glm()</code> can accommodate over-dispersion while <code>loglm()</code> cannot</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q6" value="d" id="q6d"> <label for="q6d">d) All of the above</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp6"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q7">
<h3>7. How can you extend a loglinear model for frequency tables to handle multi-way contingency tables?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q7" value="a" id="q7a"> <label for="q7a">a) By adding association terms to the model</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q7" value="b" id="q7b"> <label for="q7b">b) By fitting separate loglinear models for each combination of predictors</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q7" value="c" id="q7c"> <label for="q7c">c) By using a multivariate linear regression model</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q7" value="d" id="q7d"> <label for="q7d">d) By using a multinomial logistic regression model</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp7"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q8">
<h3>8. For a three-way frequency table, what is the interpretation of the model symbolized by <code>[A B] [A C]</code>?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q8" value="a" id="q8a"> <label for="q8a">a) A and B are conditionally independent given C</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q8" value="b" id="q8b"> <label for="q8b">b) B and C are conditionally independent given A</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q8" value="c" id="q8c"> <label for="q8c">c) A and B are mutually independent</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q8" value="d" id="q8d"> <label for="q8d">d) The association between A and B is the same for all levels of C</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp8"></div>
</div>

</form>

    incorrect: "The likelihood ratio test is the standard method for testing goodness of fit of loglinear models. The chi-square test only tests complete independence vs. any association."

  q4: {
    correct: "Logit models are designed for binary (or categorical) response variables and model the probability of an outcome.     incorrect: "The key difference is that glm() estimates parameters (regression coefficients) that quantify the effects of variables and their interactions, while loglm() focuses on fitted frequencies and overall model fit. Both use iterative methods and provide likelihood ratio tests."
